result.summary: Rhea bears children to Cronos, who swallows them, but with Earth and Heaven's help she hides Zeus in Crete and tricks Cronos with a stone. Zeus frees his siblings and uncles and gains the thunderbolt, then the line of Iapetus and the trick at Mecone are told.

scenes.title: Cronos swallows his children
scenes.summary: Rhea bears six children and Cronos swallows them to avoid being overthrown. Rhea appeals to Earth and Heaven for a plan.
scenes.stakes: Cronos fears losing his kingship to his son; Rhea faces the loss of each child.

scenes.title: Zeus hidden in Crete
scenes.summary: Earth takes the newborn Zeus to a cave in Crete and gives Cronos a swaddled stone, which he swallows.
scenes.stakes: The infant Zeus would be swallowed if the trick fails.

scenes.title: Cronos disgorges the children
scenes.summary: Grown, Zeus makes Cronos vomit up his offspring. He sets the stone at Pytho and frees his uncles, who give him thunder.
scenes.stakes: Cronos is being overthrown; Zeus seeks to secure his rule.

scenes.title: The sons of Iapetus punished
scenes.summary: Iapetus's sons receive their fates: Menoetius is struck down, Atlas holds up the sky, and Prometheus is bound until Heracles slays the eagle.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus suffers eternal torment for defying Zeus.

scenes.title: The trick at Mecone
scenes.summary: Prometheus divides an ox, hiding bones under fat to deceive Zeus. Zeus sees the trick but takes the bones, angry, and plans harm for men.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus risks Zeus's wrath; mankind risks punishment.

notable_quotes.reason: Cronos swallows the stone, unknowingly sealing his own downfall.
Explains the origin of burning bones for the gods in sacrifice.

analysis.text: Succession myth: each ruler fears and is overthrown by his son, until Zeus breaks the cycle through cunning and force.
The Mecone trick explains the human sacrifice custom and begins the conflict between Zeus and mankind.

legacy.text: The Prometheus myth shaped later works such as Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound and Shelley's Prometheus Unbound.

fun_facts.text: The stone swallowed by Cronos was said to be displayed at Delphi in antiquity.

language_notes.text: "Subject in love to Cronos" means she yielded to him as his consort; the phrase is a formal way of saying she lay with him.
"Earth-Shaker" is a standard title of Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes; he is not named here.
"Lyetus" is the same Cretan place as "Lyctus" in sentence 8, a city in Crete; the spelling varies in this translation.
"The earlier king of the gods" is Cronos, who ruled before Zeus; "son of Heaven" identifies him as Heaven's child.
"Wretch!" is the poet's exclamation about Cronos, who is foolish and pitiable for being fooled.
"Beguiled" means tricked or deceived; Earth's "deep suggestions" are her cunning counsel.
Pytho is the old name of Delphi; the stone was said to be displayed there as a sacred object.
The father's brothers are the Cyclopes, sons of Heaven, whom Heaven had imprisoned; they repay Zeus with thunder.
Epimetheus's name means 'afterthought'. He accepted Pandora, the woman Zeus formed, despite warnings from his brother Prometheus ('forethought').
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld, here used for the realm of the dead or Tartarus.
The Hesperides are nymphs who guard the golden apples in the far west, where Atlas stands at the world's edge.
'Inextricable' means impossible to untie or escape from.
Mecone (Sicyon) is the place where gods and men settled their shares of sacrificial meat, explaining the origin of sacrifice.
'Good sir' is ironic and mocking, a polite address covering Zeus's rebuke.
Explains the custom of Greek sacrifice: men burned bones and fat for the gods and kept the meat to eat.

context_notes.text: Cronos swallows his children because of a prophecy that one of them would take his kingship, as he had taken his father Heaven's.
Crete was the traditional birthplace of Zeus, who was hidden in a cave on Mount Aegeum (Aegaeon) away from Cronos.
Thunder and the thunderbolt become Zeus's chief weapons and the sign of his rule.
Iapetus was a Titan. His sons Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus and Epimetheus all suffer under Zeus or bring trouble on mankind.
Heracles, son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene, killed the eagle; his glory is thereby increased, serving Zeus's plan.

literary_notes.text: "Kept no blind outlook" figures his watchfulness as sight, showing how carefully he guarded his throne.
The audience knows Cronos has swallowed a stone, while he does not, which makes his scheme look foolish.
Closing on the thunderbolts shows Zeus's power as based on gifts and cunning, and it ends the episode on his sovereignty.
Epimetheus's acceptance of the woman anticipates the coming misery of men, which the poem develops later.
The liver regrowing each night makes the punishment vivid and endless, stressing Zeus's power over an immortal.
The deceptive dish looks rich and fine but hides bones; appearance and reality are opposed.
'Whose wisdom is everlasting' repeats a fixed description that stresses Zeus's superior intelligence against Prometheus's cunning.
'Smiling softly' and 'wily' show Prometheus as sly and self-assured, confident in his trick.
The reader learns that Zeus sees through the trick, though Prometheus believes it has worked.
